meta.title: News Feed
meta.summary: Post updates and read a personalized home timeline (Twitter / Instagram style) at very high read volume.

functional: Post a short update with optional images
Read a home timeline of followed users, newest first
nonFunctional: Home timeline loads in < 200 ms p99
New posts may take a few seconds to appear (eventual consistency)
Reads must stay available even if posting is degraded

slos.name: Timeline speed
slos.sli: Timeline requests served within the threshold, divided by all timeline requests, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Timeline availability
slos.sli: Timeline requests that succeed, divided by all timeline requests

slos.name: Post freshness
slos.sli: Posts visible in followers' timelines within the threshold, divided by all posts

alerts.when: Timeline errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: People cannot read their feed. This is the main product.

alerts.when: p99 timeline latency above 200 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Slow feeds drive people away even when nothing is failing.

alerts.when: Age of the oldest fan-out message above 30 seconds for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Timelines go stale long before anyone sees an error, so this is the earliest warning.

alerts.when: Timeline cache memory above 85%, or evictions rising
alerts.why: Evicted timelines have to be rebuilt from the database, which is slow and expensive.

alerts.when: Fan-out worker failure rate above 1% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Failed deliveries leave some followers without the post until the retry succeeds.

signals.name: Age of the oldest message
signals.why: How far behind fan-out is, and so how stale timelines are.

signals.name: Evictions per second
signals.why: Shows memory pressure before timelines start missing.

signals.name: Throttled requests
signals.why: A viral post creates read spikes on a few keys.

steps: Open a slow trace: is the time in the cache read, the post lookup or the celebrity merge?
Check the timeline cache hit ratio and evictions.
Check posts store throttling: a viral post makes hot keys.
Count how many celebrity accounts the user follows: their posts are merged at read time.
Check the fan-out queue age first: it is the best single indicator.
Look at worker failures and retries.
Check follower graph latency: fan-out pages through followers.
For celebrities, posts are not fanned out, so check the read-time merge path instead.

flows.title: Post an update
flows.summary: Write path with fan-out on write: store the post once, then push its id into every follower's cached timeline in the background.

steps.label: resolve feed.example.com
steps.detail: The app resolves the API hostname, which points at the CDN. The answer is cached on the phone and by resolvers.

steps.label: POST /api/posts
steps.detail: Images were already uploaded separately; the post references them by id.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: Writes are never cached; the CDN forwards them to the origin.

steps.label: route
steps.detail: Stateless Post Service instances sit behind the load balancer.

steps.label: PutItem post
steps.detail: The post id is a time-sortable Snowflake-style id (timestamp + machine + sequence), so ids sort by time without a global counter.

steps.label: OK
steps.detail: The post is durable. Everything after this point can be retried.

steps.label: publish PostCreated
steps.detail: Fan-out is slow for popular authors, so it happens off the request path.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: The author gets an immediate response.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: Back out through the edge.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: The client shows the post in the author's own timeline right away, even before fan-out finishes.

steps.label: deliver PostCreated
steps.detail: Workers scale with queue depth. A celebrity post does not slow down anyone's request.

steps.label: GET followers(42) page 1
steps.detail: Followers are read in pages of a few thousand.

steps.label: SELECT follower_id
5,000 ids
steps.detail: Index on (followee_id, follower_id) makes this a range scan.

steps.label: followers page
steps.detail: Inactive followers (no login for 30 days) are skipped to save cache memory; their timeline is rebuilt when they return.

steps.label: LPUSH + LTRIM ×N
steps.detail: Fan-out on write: one small write per follower, pipelined. Each list is trimmed to ~800 ids so memory stays bounded.
steps.payload:
MULTI
LPUSH timeline:1001 1857261298011340800
LTRIM timeline:1001 0 799
…
EXEC

flows.title: Read home timeline
flows.summary: Read path: precomputed ids from cache, merged with posts from celebrities that were deliberately not fanned out.

steps.label: private: pass through
steps.detail: Timelines are per-user, so the CDN does not cache them. It still serves every image and video in them.

steps.label: LRANGE timeline:1001 0 49
steps.detail: The timeline was built ahead of time by fan-out, so reading it is one memory lookup.

steps.label: 50 post ids
steps.detail: Sub-millisecond. This is why fan-out on write pays off: reads outnumber writes ~100:1.

steps.label: celebrities I follow
steps.detail: Hybrid model: accounts with more than ~100k followers are not fanned out, since one post would mean millions of cache writes. Their posts are pulled at read time instead.

steps.label: [nasa, elonmusk]
steps.detail: This list is small and heavily cached.

steps.label: BatchGet + recent celeb posts
steps.detail: Hydrate the 50 ids into full posts and fetch the latest posts by followed celebrities.

steps.label: merge by time
steps.detail: Merge the two sorted lists by post id (which is time-ordered), then apply ranking if the product has one.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: Media URLs point at the CDN, so images load from the edge.

steps.label: HIT
steps.detail: Popular media is almost always cached at the edge.

notes.text: Fan-out on write makes reads cheap but writes expensive; fan-out on read is the opposite. The hybrid (write for normal users, read for celebrities) is the standard answer.
200M users × 800 ids × 8 bytes ≈ 1.3 TB. Use a Redis cluster sharded by user id, and only keep timelines for recently active users.
If fan-out falls behind, timelines are a few seconds stale but reads keep working. The queue absorbs bursts like a celebrity post.
Time-sortable ids (Snowflake style) avoid a central counter and let timelines merge and paginate by id.
Media is most of the bytes. Serving it from the CDN keeps the origin small.
